stops.title: Old Port — La Rochelle's gateway
stops.text: Begin at the Vieux-Port, the setting that explains almost everything about La Rochelle. The city grew as an Atlantic trading port and became wealthy, independent and strategically important. Three medieval towers once guarded the harbour entrance: the Tour de la Chaîne, Tour Saint-Nicolas and Tour de la Lanterne. Look across the water and imagine the heavy chain that was stretched between the Chain Tower and Saint-Nicolas to close the harbour at night. The harbour was also central to the city's later conflict with the French crown. After the Protestant city surrendered during the Great Siege of 1627–1628, much of the landward defences were demolished, while the great seafront towers survived. Today the same harbour is still the heart of the city, but the military waterfront has become a place for cafés, boats and strolling. It is an excellent orientation point before you decide how much of the tour you have time to see.
stops.tip: Flat; excellent place to pause. Tower interiors are optional.

stops.title: Tour de la Chaîne and Cours des Dames
stops.text: The Tour de la Chaîne dates from the fourteenth century and was one half of the harbour-closing mechanism. The chain was attached here and stretched to the much larger Tour Saint-Nicolas. The tower also served later as a powder store. From the Cours des Dames, look back at the tower and notice how a formidable defensive building now sits among restaurants and everyday city life. That mixture is characteristic of La Rochelle: its historic buildings have not been isolated from the modern town. If you are interested in going inside, treat the visit as an optional extra. The important story can be understood perfectly well from outside, and the tower involves stairs.
stops.tip: Flat outside. Interior is optional and stair-heavy.

stops.title: Tour de la Lanterne — lighthouse and prison
stops.text: The Tour de la Lanterne is the oldest surviving lighthouse tower on the Atlantic coast of France. The present tower was built in the fifteenth century, replacing an earlier structure. Its name refers to the lantern that was lit to guide ships. It later became a prison, and its walls preserve hundreds of inscriptions left by prisoners, especially in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. For this walking tour, the exterior is enough: the tower marks the western end of the historic harbour and the line of the old seaward defences. If you decide to enter, regard it as an optional extension because the climb is substantial. The tower is particularly worthwhile if you enjoy the human details of history — the prisoners' marks make the past unusually tangible.
stops.tip: Flat outside. Interior requires many stairs.

stops.title: Grosse Horloge — from city gate to town clock
stops.text: The Grosse Horloge began as a fortified gateway in the medieval wall separating the town from the port. Originally there were separate openings for carts and pedestrians. A clock and bell were added in the fifteenth century, and later rebuilding produced the elegant upper structure you see today. Notice the change as you pass from the harbour side into the dense old town. The gateway is therefore more than a photogenic monument: it marks a surviving boundary between two parts of medieval La Rochelle. It is also a useful navigation landmark. If you are improvising the route, seeing the Grosse Horloge usually means you are right at the edge of the most interesting part of the historic centre.
stops.tip: Flat and pedestrian-friendly; avoid stopping directly under the arch when busy.
stops.credit: Jean-Christophe BENOIST / Wikimedia Commons — CC BY 3.0

stops.title: Église Saint-Sauveur — the old harbour church
stops.text: Saint-Sauveur stands close to the old commercial heart of La Rochelle. The church's history reflects the city's repeated rebuilding and religious upheavals. Its position is more important to the walking tour than its architectural grandeur: it sits where the harbour, the old trading streets and the dense medieval town come together. Look at the surrounding streets and imagine the movement of merchants, sailors and goods that once concentrated here. La Rochelle's religious history also changed dramatically during the Reformation and the later restoration of Catholic institutions after the Great Siege. Even if the church itself is closed, the exterior and the surrounding streets provide a useful chapter in the story of a city whose fortunes were tied closely to both commerce and belief.
stops.tip: Flat; exterior stop. Treat interior access as optional.

stops.title: The arcaded streets — practical elegance
stops.text: Now look at the streets rather than searching for one particular monument. La Rochelle is famous for its arcades: covered passages beneath houses along important commercial streets. They protected pedestrians and shopkeepers from Atlantic rain and strong sun while providing useful space for commerce. The city's prosperity is visible in the mixture of buildings around you — timber-framed houses, pale stone façades and grander merchant residences. This is one of the pleasures of La Rochelle: its historic character is spread through ordinary streets rather than concentrated in a single museum. Walk slowly beneath the arcades and look up at the upper floors, doorways and carved details. You will often find something interesting without needing to go anywhere in particular.
stops.tip: Very flat. Ideal for a slow, flexible section.

stops.title: Hôtel de Ville — power, independence and the Great Siege
stops.text: La Rochelle's Hôtel de Ville has an extraordinary claim: a town hall has stood here since 1298, making it the oldest French town hall still in use. The building was largely rebuilt around 1490 in a deliberately fortified style, with crenellations, machicolations and a corner tower. That appearance reflects the city's unusual municipal independence and confidence. La Rochelle later became a major Protestant stronghold. The most dramatic chapter came in 1627–1628, when royal forces under Cardinal Richelieu besieged the city. Mayor Jean Guiton became a symbol of resistance. The building suffered a major fire in 2013 and was reopened after extensive restoration in 2019. Spend a little time looking at the square as well as the building: this is one of the best places to understand the political history of La Rochelle.
stops.tip: Flat; the square provides good places to pause.

stops.title: Place de l'Hôtel de Ville — Jean Guiton and the siege
stops.text: Use this square as a short companion to the Hôtel de Ville. The Great Siege of 1627–1628 is one of the defining episodes in La Rochelle's history. The city was a Protestant stronghold resisting the authority of the French crown. Royal forces built a massive line of fortifications around the city and a sea barrier to prevent supplies arriving. Jean Guiton, one of the city's leading figures, became associated with the determination to resist. The siege ended with surrender, starvation and a profound change in the city's political position. The episode explains why La Rochelle's medieval independence did not survive intact into the modern period. It also explains why the city's harbour towers and surviving walls have such a strong historical presence.
stops.tip: Flat; use as a short stop if time is tight.

stops.title: Renaissance merchant quarter — Atlantic wealth
stops.text: Here the city's commercial success becomes architectural. Wealthy merchants and shipowners built substantial houses with courtyards, elaborate façades and carved details. La Rochelle's Atlantic connections brought goods, people and ideas from far beyond the immediate region. That prosperity also has a darker history. The city participated in Atlantic colonial trade, including the slave trade, and some merchant families accumulated wealth through it. Modern heritage interpretation increasingly places those uncomfortable facts alongside the more familiar story of maritime prosperity. As you look at the grand houses, remember that historic architecture can record both commercial achievement and the unequal systems that produced it. This is a good example of why a city guide should not merely point at attractive buildings but explain the society that created them.
stops.tip: Flat; a good optional section when you have 90 minutes or more.

stops.title: Saint-Louis Cathedral — Protestant La Rochelle becomes Catholic again
stops.text: Saint-Louis Cathedral is a useful reminder that La Rochelle's religious history was anything but simple. During the Reformation the city became a major centre of French Protestantism. After the Great Siege and the defeat of the Huguenot city, Catholic institutions were restored and the religious landscape changed dramatically. The cathedral occupies a site associated with that transition. If it is open, you can look inside; if not, the exterior still makes a useful stop because the building helps explain the religious and political transformation of La Rochelle. The story is not simply about Catholics and Protestants: it is about royal power, municipal independence and the changing identity of France.
stops.tip: Flat outside. Interior depends on opening/access.

availability.note: Exterior always available; interior hours should be checked locally.

stops.title: Musée du Nouveau Monde — La Rochelle and the Atlantic world
stops.text: The Musée du Nouveau Monde explores La Rochelle's long connection with the Americas. The subject is particularly important because the port was deeply involved in Atlantic commerce. The museum's collections include material relating to trade, migration, colonial societies and the relationships between Europe and the Americas. You do not need to enter to understand the significance of the building's presence in the old town, but an interior visit can be worthwhile if your time allows and the museum is open. For this tour, it is deliberately a medium-priority stop: interesting, but not so essential that a short visit should be held up by a closure or queue.
stops.tip: Flat approach. Interior is optional; the museum is not fully accessible to wheelchair users according to its official information.

stops.title: Central Market — La Rochelle alive today
stops.text: The Marché Central changes the tone of the tour. Instead of looking at a monument, listen to the city functioning today. The present market hall dates from 1834 and remains a working food market. Its large glazed areas, zinc roofing, clock and small bell turret are practical rather than monumental. On market mornings the surrounding streets also fill with stalls. This is one of the best places to see that La Rochelle is a living town rather than a heritage display. If your visit is on a market morning, browsing may be more enjoyable than listening to every word, so the app treats this as a flexible stop rather than a compulsory lecture.
stops.tip: Completely flat. Can be crowded, particularly Wednesday and Saturday mornings.
stops.credit: Patrick Despoix / Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 3.0

stops.title: Place de Verdun — the northern edge of the historic centre
stops.text: Place de Verdun is useful as a geographical hinge. From here the old centre opens toward the northern part of La Rochelle, while the historic core remains close at hand. It is not one of the city's headline monuments, so the guide uses it as an optional connector. If you have plenty of time, it provides a change of scene and a useful point from which to reach the Muséum and Jardin des Plantes. If you are running late, this is one of the first sections the planner will remove.
stops.tip: Flat. Primarily a connector and optional stop.

stops.title: Muséum d'Histoire naturelle — science and empire
stops.text: The Muséum d'Histoire naturelle is worth considering because its collections tell a different story from the harbour and fortifications. La Rochelle's museums preserve natural-history collections connected with exploration, collecting and scientific exchange. The building and collections also provide a route into a more complicated history of European encounters with other parts of the world. If you enjoy museums, this can easily become a longer visit than the audio section suggests. The app therefore treats the five-minute audio description as an introduction rather than a substitute for entering the museum. If your available time is short, the planner will normally favour the old harbour and old town first.
stops.tip: Flat approach. Interior has opening hours and should be checked.

stops.title: Jardin des Plantes — a quiet change of pace
stops.text: The Jardin des Plantes offers a welcome change from stone streets and harbour architecture. The garden preserves memories of La Rochelle's scientific and maritime connections, including plants associated with expeditions and botanical collecting. It is also simply a pleasant place to pause. The city keeps the garden open for long hours, and in October the closing time is still early evening rather than late at night. This makes it a useful flexible component of the tour: if you have time and want a quieter experience, come in; if your ship's departure or your return to the hotel is approaching, it is easy to skip.
stops.tip: Flat and restful. Good place for a seated break.

stops.title: Chapelle des Dames Blanches — a small cultural surprise
stops.text: The Chapelle des Dames Blanches is a smaller and more contemporary stop. A former chapel near the old port has been used as a gallery and cultural space, taking advantage of its high ceilings, stained glass and distinctive light. It illustrates a useful theme in La Rochelle: historic buildings are often given new lives rather than preserved as static monuments. If an exhibition is open, you may find it worth a brief look inside. If it is closed, the building can simply be treated as an exterior point and the tour can continue. This is deliberately a low-priority stop so that the main historical story does not depend on it.
stops.tip: Flat. Opening is seasonal; treat as an optional bonus.

stops.title: Bassin des Chalutiers and Musée Maritime
stops.text: The Bassin des Chalutiers shows La Rochelle as a working maritime city rather than only a medieval one. The Musée Maritime and the vessels around the basin tell the story of fishing, shipping and the city's more recent relationship with the Atlantic. This stop is deliberately optional because the museum itself can take much longer than the audio description. Even if you do not enter, the basin provides an excellent waterfront perspective and gives context to the modern port economy. It is also a useful alternative destination if the medieval towers are busy or temporarily inaccessible.
stops.tip: Flat waterfront. Museum entry can consume substantial time.

stops.title: Porte des Deux Moulins and the seaward walls
stops.text: The Porte des Deux Moulins is a useful reminder that La Rochelle was a fortified town beyond the famous harbour towers. This stretch of the waterfront preserves the relationship between the old defensive line and the sea. Rather than concentrating on one building, look along the walls and consider how the city once controlled movement through a narrow defended perimeter. This is also a pleasant place to experience the Atlantic edge without the crowds that gather around the main harbour entrance. It makes a good optional extension for a longer tour and can be omitted without damaging the central historical story.
stops.tip: Mostly flat, but some waterfront surfaces can be uneven.
